ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections):
Overview — otitis (ear infections)
Infection/inflammation of the ear — the external canal (otitis externa) and the middle ear (otitis media, acute and with effusion). Mostly clinical diagnoses on otoscopy.
The organising principle: localise the problem. Canal (OE — pain on moving the tragus/pinna, discharge) vs middle ear behind an intact drum (AOM — bulging red drum; glue ear — retracted dull drum + effusion). Malignant OE is a dangerous skull-base extension in diabetics/immunocompromised.

What & Why

Acute otitis media is acute infection/inflammation of the middle ear (the air-filled space behind the tympanic membrane housing the ossicles). It’s one of the commonest infections of childhood (the classic “child with ear pain after a cold”); most are self-limiting (so antibiotic stewardship is central), but the rare complications (mastoiditis, intracranial spread) are serious. Core: the otoscopy picture (bulging red drum), the antibiotic decision rules, and the complications.

The core mechanism: the Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx. A viral URTI → Eustachian tube dysfunction/oedema → the middle ear can’t drain/ventilate → bacteria ascend from the nasopharynx → infection with pus under pressure. This is why AOM follows a cold and why children (short, horizontal Eustachian tubes) are prone.
Organisms: often preceded by a viral URTI; commonest bacteria are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae (also Moraxella catarrhalis).
Clinical Features
  • Otalgia (ear pain) — infants/young children may rub or tug at the ear, be irritable, feed poorly, or have fever
  • Reduced hearing in the affected ear (conductive — fluid/pus behind the drum)
  • URTI symptoms — cough, coryza, sore throat (often preceding)
  • Vertigo/balance problems if the vestibular system is involved
  • If the tympanic membrane perforates → discharge (otorrhoea) — often with sudden relief of pain (pressure released)
Investigations — Otoscopy
📷 Image placeholder — Otoscopy of acute otitis media — a bulging, erythematous, opacified tympanic membrane with loss of the light reflex (the hallmark)

The diagnosis is clinical, made on otoscopy (normal TM = pearly grey, translucent, slightly shiny, with a light reflex):

  • Bulging tympanic membrane with loss of the light reflex (the hallmark)
  • Erythema and opacification of the TM
  • Loss of the normal landmarks (malleus handle obscured)
  • Perforation with purulent discharge (if ruptured)
  • Air-fluid level / bubbles behind the drum
Management
Most cases resolve without antibiotics — symptoms usually settle within ~3 days (~60% improve within 24 h). Analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen) is the mainstay.
ApproachWhen
No antibiotic (safety-net)Most children >2 years, unilateral, not systemically unwell
Delayed (“back-up”) prescriptionUse after 3 days if symptoms haven’t improved or worsen
Immediate antibioticSystemically unwell; significant comorbidity; immunocompromised; <2 years with bilateral AOM; otorrhoea/perforation
💊 Antibiotic choice
  • First-line: amoxicillin, 5–7 days — hook: Acute Otitis Media → Amoxicillin
  • Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin
  • Pregnancy (if macrolide needed): erythromycin
  • Second-line / failure: co-amoxiclav
🔔 Safety-net & escalate
  • Return if symptoms worsen rapidly, don’t improve in 3 days, discharge begins, or the child becomes systemically very unwell
  • Admit / urgent referral if severe systemic infection or a suspected complication (mastoiditis, meningitis, intracranial abscess, facial palsy)
Complications
  • Tympanic membrane perforation → otorrhoea — usually heals; if perforation + discharge persists >2 weeks (NICE CKS) → chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM)
  • Hearing loss (conductive; usually temporary); labyrinthitis (→ vertigo)
  • Mastoiditis — spread to the mastoid air cells → postauricular swelling/erythema/tenderness, a protruding auricle, systemic illness → IV antibiotics ± mastoidectomy
  • Intracranial spread (rare, life-threatening): meningitis, intracranial/extradural abscess, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST), facial nerve palsy
  • Glue ear (otitis media with effusion) — persistent middle-ear fluid → conductive hearing loss; cholesteatoma (with chronic disease)

What it is
Middle-ear infection, usually post-viral-URTI; commonest bugs Strep pneumoniae + H. influenzae.
Presentation
Child with ear pain (tugging ear) + fever + reduced hearing after a cold.
Otoscopy
BULGING, red/opaque TM with LOSS OF LIGHT REFLEX (± perforation with discharge).
Perforation

Systemically unwell, comorbid/immunocompromised, <2 years with BILATERAL AOM, or otorrhoea/perforation.
Antibiotic
Amoxicillin 5–7 days (“AOM = AMoxicillin”); clarithromycin if allergic; erythromycin in pregnancy.
CSOM
Perforation + otorrhoea >6 weeks.
Key complication
Mastoiditis (postauricular swelling/tenderness + protruding ear); also meningitis, abscess, CVST, facial palsy.
What & Why

Otitis externa is inflammation of the skin of the external auditory canal (the “outer” ear infection, aka “swimmer’s ear”). It’s common and usually simple — treated with topical drops, not oral antibiotics — but must be distinguished from otitis media, and carries one rare but life-threatening variant: malignant (necrotising) otitis externa, which spreads to the skull base in diabetic/immunocompromised patients.

The core mechanism: the ear canal is protected by cerumen (acidic, water-repellent) + intact skin. Anything that breaches this — water (raises pH, macerates skin), trauma (cotton buds), or wax removal — lets bacteria/fungi invade the canal skin. So the risk factors are all “things that damage the canal’s defences”.
Organisms: Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus are commonest; fungal (Candida/Aspergillus — otomycosis) especially after multiple courses of topical antibiotics.
Risk Factors
  • Swimming / water exposure (“swimmer’s ear” — moisture macerates the canal)
  • Trauma to the canal — cotton buds, earplugs, hearing aids (wax is protective; disrupting it raises risk)
  • Multiple courses of topical antibiotics → fungal (Candida) superinfection
  • Eczema/psoriasis/seborrhoeic dermatitis of the canal, a narrow canal, diabetes/immunocompromise
Clinical Features
  • Ear pain (otalgia) — often worse on moving the tragus/pinna or inserting an otoscope
  • Itchiness (prominent, especially fungal); discharge (otorrhoea)
  • Conductive hearing loss if the canal occludes (swelling/debris)
  • On exam: erythema + swelling of the canal, tenderness, pus/discharge/debris, regional lymphadenopathy; the TM may be obscured (try to visualise it — exclude perforation/OM)

Management — Simple OE
  • Analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen) — pain can be significant
  • Aural toilet — microsuction/cleaning of debris improves drop penetration (a key, often-overlooked step)
  • Topical antibiotic ± corticosteroid ear drops — the mainstay (e.g. ciprofloxacin + dexamethasone, or gentamicin/neomycin + steroid), typically 7 days
  • Avoid aminoglycoside drops (gentamicin/neomycin) if the TM is perforated (ototoxicity) — use a non-ototoxic agent (e.g. ciprofloxacin)
  • Topical antifungal (e.g. clotrimazole) if fungal (otomycosis); acetic acid 2% spray for mild cases
  • Keep the ear dry, avoid cotton buds; ear swab if resistant/recurrent
  • Oral antibiotics are NOT routinely needed (topical is superior) — reserve for spreading infection/cellulitis, systemic illness, diabetes/immunocompromise
Management — Malignant (Necrotising) OE
  • Urgent ENT referral/admission for severe/unresolving OE with disproportionate pain, especially in a diabetic/immunocompromised patient
  • CT (± MRI) to assess temporal-bone/skull-base osteomyelitis
  • IV antipseudomonal antibiotics — ciprofloxacin (prolonged, weeks) — hook: “cipro moe the lawn” (ciprofloxacin for MOE, Pseudomonas = the green “lawn”)
  • Meticulous glucose control, aural toilet/debridement; hyperbaric oxygen in selected cases; monitor for cranial nerve involvement (facial first, then IX/X/XI)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Inflammation of the EAR CANAL skin (“swimmer’s ear”); Pseudomonas + Staph (fungal if recurrent/post-antibiotics).
Distinguishing sign
Pain WORSE ON MOVING THE TRAGUS/PINNA (vs otitis media), itch, discharge, red swollen tender canal.
Risk factors
Water, trauma (cotton buds), wax removal, dermatitis.
Management
Analgesia + aural toilet + TOPICAL antibiotic ± steroid drops (7 days); topical antifungal if fungal.
Cautions
Avoid aminoglycoside drops if TM perforated (ototoxic). Oral antibiotics NOT routine.
Malignant OE
Elderly DIABETIC/immunocompromised + severe unremitting pain + GRANULATION TISSUE → skull-base osteomyelitis + cranial nerve palsy (facial first).
MOE management
CT/MRI + urgent ENT + IV ciprofloxacin (“cipro moe the lawn”) + glucose control.
Organism
Pseudomonas aeruginosa = the bug in both swimmer’s ear and MOE.
What & Why

Malignant otitis externa (MOE), better called necrotising otitis externa (NOE), is a rare, aggressive, potentially fatal infection in which otitis externa spreads from the ear canal into the temporal bone and skull base, causing osteomyelitis. It’s a must-not-miss ENT emergency: almost exclusively in elderly diabetics and the immunocompromised, easily mistaken for ordinary OE, and untreated it progresses to cranial nerve palsies, intracranial spread, and death. “Malignant” reflects aggressive, destructive behaviour — it is NOT a cancer.

The core mechanism: infection (almost always Pseudomonas aeruginosa) starts in the external canal and spreads through the osseocartilaginous junction + fissures of Santorini into the skull base → progressive osteomyelitis. Diabetic microvascular disease + impaired immunity are why this population is uniquely vulnerable. As osteomyelitis advances, it reaches the cranial nerve foramina → cranial neuropathies (facial nerve first).

The red-flag triad: elderly diabetic + severe pain out of proportion + granulation tissue in the canal = MOE until proven otherwise.
Risk Factors & Organism
👤 Risk factors
  • Diabetes mellitus (the classic — especially poorly controlled) — the dominant risk factor
  • Immunocompromise (HIV, chemotherapy, immunosuppressants, elderly)
  • Preceding otitis externa (± ear syringing/trauma in a diabetic); older age
🦠 Organism
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa — >90% of cases (the exam answer)
  • Occasionally Staph aureus (incl. MRSA); rarely fungal (Aspergillus, Candida) — consider if not responding, especially if profoundly immunocompromised
Clinical Features
  • Severe, deep, unremitting otalgia — classically worse at night and out of proportion to otoscopic findings
  • Persistent otorrhoea not settling with topical treatment
  • Granulation tissue in the canal (classically at the bony-cartilaginous junction on the floor) — the hallmark sign
  • Headache, temporomandibular/periauricular pain, pain on chewing; systemic fever/malaise (variable)
  • Cranial nerve palsies as it advances: facial nerve (CN VII) first + commonest (through the temporal bone), then IX, X, XI (jugular foramen syndrome)
Investigations
  • Bloods: raised inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR, WCC), glucose/HbA1c (often poorly controlled diabetes) — ESR/CRP used to monitor response
  • Microbiology — ear swab / canal biopsy for culture + sensitivities — essential to guide antibiotics (detect ciprofloxacin-resistant Pseudomonas); biopsy granulation tissue to exclude malignancy (SCC)
  • CT (temporal bones) — first-line: bony erosion / skull-base osteomyelitis + extent
  • MRI — best for soft-tissue + intracranial extension; used to monitor
  • Radionuclide scans — technetium-99m bone scan (sensitive, non-specific) + gallium-67 (tracks active infection; monitors resolution and guides duration)
Management
  • Urgent ENT referral and admission
  • Prolonged IV antipseudomonal antibiotics — ciprofloxacin (± an antipseudomonal beta-lactam e.g. ceftazidime / piperacillin-tazobactam), culture-guided, typically ~6 weeks (up to ~3 months), guided by inflammatory markers + gallium scanning (“cipro moe the lawn”)
  • Be aware of ciprofloxacin-resistant Pseudomonas → adjust to sensitivities (e.g. ceftazidime)
  • Strict glycaemic control + correct immunosuppression where possible — central to recovery
  • Aural toilet / debridement; surgical debridement reserved for granulation tissue/sequestra or non-response (surgery is not the mainstay — antibiotics are); hyperbaric oxygen in refractory cases
  • MDT care (ENT, microbiology/ID, endocrinology ± ophthalmology/neurology); long-term follow-up (recurrence recognised)
Complications
  • Skull-base osteomyelitis (the defining process)
  • Cranial nerve palsies (facial → IX/X/XI) — may be permanent
  • Meningitis, intracranial/brain abscess, dural venous sinus thrombosis
  • Death (mortality remains significant even with treatment)
Exam Pearls
What it is
OE spreading to the temporal bone/skull base → osteomyelitis; NOT a cancer (“malignant” = aggressive behaviour).
Red-flag triad
Elderly DIABETIC + severe pain out of proportion (worse at night) + GRANULATION TISSUE in the canal.
Organism
Pseudomonas aeruginosa (>90%).
Nerves
Facial nerve (VII) = first/commonest, then IX/X/XI.
Investigations
Raised CRP/ESR, glucose/HbA1c; ear swab + biopsy (culture, exclude SCC); CT (bone erosion) + MRI; gallium/technetium scans to confirm & monitor.
Management
Urgent ENT admission + prolonged IV antipseudomonal (ciprofloxacin ± ceftazidime, culture-guided, ~6 wks) + tight glucose control.
Currency
Watch for ciprofloxacin-resistant Pseudomonas.
Rule
Ordinary OE not improving in a diabetic → think MOE.
What & Why

Otitis media with effusion (OME), or “glue ear”, is a collection of fluid in the middle ear WITHOUT signs of acute infection. It’s the commonest cause of acquired (conductive) hearing loss in childhood and the commonest reason for elective surgery in children — and persistent hearing loss can cause speech, language, behavioural, and educational problems at a critical developmental stage. Core: it’s fluid + hearing loss (not infection), most resolve spontaneously (active observation first), and grommets are the key intervention if it persists.

The core mechanism: the Eustachian tube ventilates/drains the middle ear. If dysfunctional (immature in young children, or blocked by adenoidal hypertrophy or after a URTI/AOM) → negative pressure → transudation of fluid, which becomes thick and “glue-like” → dampens ossicular movement → conductive hearing loss.
Risk Factors
  • Male sex; siblings with glue ear / family history
  • Bottle-feeding (breastfeeding is protective)
  • Day-care/nursery attendance (more URTIs); parental smoking (passive smoke)
  • Winter/spring season, atopy, recent AOM/URTI
  • Down syndrome and cleft palate (much higher prevalence, 60–85%) — a special group
Clinical Features
  • Peaks around 2 years of age
  • Hearing loss is the presenting feature — conductive; may show as inattention, “not listening”, turning up the TV, speech/language delay, or poor school performance
  • Commonest cause of conductive hearing loss AND of elective surgery in children
  • Secondary problems: speech and language delay, behavioural problems, balance problems
  • Usually NO pain, fever, or discharge (distinguishes from AOM — this is fluid, not acute infection)
Investigations
  • Otoscopy: fluid visible behind an intact tympanic membrane — a dull/retracted drum, sometimes with air-fluid levels or bubbles + loss of the light reflex. NO discharge, NO bulging, NO marked redness (those suggest AOM)
  • Tympanometry — a flat (“type B”) trace (no middle-ear compliance) confirms an effusion
  • Pure-tone audiometry (age-appropriate) — documents the conductive hearing loss + severity
  • Confirm on 2 occasions ~6–12 weeks apart before acting (many resolve)
Referral Criteria
  • ALL adults with unilateral OME → 2-week-wait referral — a one-sided adult effusion can be caused by a postnasal space tumour (nasopharyngeal carcinoma) obstructing the Eustachian tube
  • Child with persistent significant hearing loss confirmed on 2 separate occasions (6–12 weeks apart)
  • Child with Down syndrome or cleft palate → refer directly (active observation is NOT appropriate — needs specialist/audiology surveillance)
  • Earlier referral if significant developmental/social/educational impact
Management
1. Active observation (first-line): a first presentation → active observation for ~3 months — most resolve spontaneously. Consider auto-inflation (Otovent balloon) during observation.
🦻 Non-surgical (if persistent)
  • Hearing aids — an alternative to surgery (especially if surgery declined/contraindicated)
  • Antibiotics, decongestants, antihistamines, and steroids are NOT recommended (ineffective)
🔧 Surgical (persistent + impact)
  • Grommets (ventilation tubes) — inserted into the TM to ventilate the middle ear (do the Eustachian tube’s job); most extrude after ~10 months. Risks: perforation, tympanosclerosis, infection/discharge
  • Adenoidectomy — adjunct to grommets (removes adenoidal obstruction), unless there’s a palate abnormality (can worsen velopharyngeal function in cleft palate)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Middle-ear fluid WITHOUT acute infection → conductive hearing loss (no pain/fever/discharge).
Epidemiology
Commonest cause of acquired hearing loss AND elective surgery in children; peaks ~2 years.
Presentation
Hearing loss / inattention / speech-language delay (not pain).
Otoscopy
Dull retracted drum, fluid/bubbles behind an INTACT membrane (no bulging/discharge). Tympanometry: flat “type B” trace.
Adult red flag
ALL adults with unilateral OME → 2WW referral (exclude nasopharyngeal carcinoma).
Special groups
Down syndrome / cleft palate → refer directly (no active observation).
Management
Active observation ~3 months (most resolve) → hearing aids or grommets (± adenoidectomy).
Grommets
Ventilate the middle ear; extrude in ~10 months. Adenoidectomy adjunct — avoid if palate abnormality.
Don’t work
Antibiotics/decongestants/antihistamines/steroids.
ENT__Hearing Loss:
Overview — hearing loss
Reduced hearing, classified as conductive (outer/middle ear) or sensorineural (cochlea/nerve). Weber & Rinne plus audiometry localise the lesion.
The organising principle: conductive vs sensorineural. Conductive (wax, otosclerosis, effusion) → Rinne negative (BC>AC), Weber to the affected ear; sensorineural (presbycusis, SNHL) → Rinne positive, Weber to the better ear. Sudden SNHL is an emergency.

Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is an ENT emergency — same-day audiometry + high-dose steroids. Unilateral tinnitus/SNHL warrants MRI to exclude an acoustic neuroma. (Cross-ref Neurology.)
What & Why

SSNHL is a rapid-onset sensorineural hearing loss developing over ≤72 hours, unexplained by other causes. It’s a true otological emergency: hearing loss becomes permanent if not treated early, yet with prompt steroids ~half of patients recover — so the window to intervene is short and every hour of delay costs recovery. A proportion hide a serious underlying cause (notably an acoustic neuroma or stroke), so it always warrants investigation. Exam essence: recognise it fast, exclude the sinister causes (MRI), and start high-dose steroids immediately.

The core distinction to nail: SSNHL is sensorineural (cochlea/CN VIII) — not a wax plug or middle-ear problem. So the first job at the bedside is to prove it’s sensorineural, not conductive (Weber/Rinne + otoscopy) — a sudden conductive loss (wax, effusion) is not this emergency.
Definition & Diagnostic Criteria
  • Sensorineural hearing loss developing over ≤72 hours, with no other explanation
  • Audiometric criterion: a loss of ≥30 dB across 3 consecutive (contiguous) frequencies — the exact definition
  • Often unilateral; may be permanent
  • Often accompanied by tinnitus and/or vertigo / aural fullness
The Decisive Fork — Idiopathic vs Identifiable Cause
Most cases are idiopathic (~85–90%) — but you must screen for the treatable/serious ones.
CategoryCauses
IdiopathicCommonest (~90%) — presumed viral / vascular / autoimmune
InfectiveViral (mumps, HSV, VZV), meningitis, syphilis, Lyme

A sudden unilateral SNHL, especially with tinnitus/imbalance, must have an acoustic neuroma excluded — the highest-yield “don’t miss”.
Clinical Assessment
  • History: onset/timescale (≤72 h), uni- vs bilateral, associated tinnitus/vertigo/aural fullness, preceding illness, drugs, trauma, neurological symptoms
  • Otoscopy — normal (excludes wax/effusion/perforation causing a conductive loss)
  • Weber’s & Rinne’s — confirm sensorineural: Weber lateralises to the unaffected (better) ear; Rinne positive (AC > BC) bilaterally
  • Neurological exam — cranial nerves (especially V, VII, VIII), cerebellar signs (posterior circulation stroke, CPA lesion)
Investigations
  • Pure-tone audiometry — establishes/confirms the diagnosis (documents the ≥30 dB loss over 3 consecutive frequencies)
  • MRI (internal auditory meatus / IAM) — to exclude an acoustic neuroma / retrocochlear pathology; done in all cases (± stroke/demyelination assessment)
  • Bloods as guided: FBC, ESR/CRP, autoimmune screen, syphilis serology, glucose (diabetes = risk/poor prognostic factor)
  • Tympanometry (confirm normal middle ear)
Management
SSNHL is an emergency — refer to ENT immediately (within 24 hours) and start treatment ASAP; don’t wait for the MRI.
  • High-dose oral corticosteroids — first-line for all cases (e.g. prednisolone, tapering). Start as early as possible — best in the first 2 weeks; little benefit beyond ~6 weeks
  • Intratympanic steroids — salvage therapy (if oral steroids fail/incomplete), or primary where systemic steroids are contraindicated (e.g. diabetes)
  • Hyperbaric oxygen — an adjunct within ~2 weeks (or salvage within a month) in some centres
  • Treat the underlying cause if identified — antivirals/antibiotics for infection, manage demyelination/Ménière’s, stop ototoxic drugs
  • Audiology follow-up — repeat audiometry; hearing aids / rehabilitation if permanent
Prognosis
  • ~50–65% recover some hearing; recovery often within the first 2 weeks
  • Worse prognostic factors: older age, severe/profound loss, presence of vertigo, delayed treatment, high-frequency (vs low-frequency) loss, diabetes
Exam Pearls
What it is
Sensorineural loss over ≤72 h; audiometric criterion ≥30 dB across 3 consecutive frequencies. OTOLOGICAL EMERGENCY.
Pattern
Usually unilateral; often idiopathic (~90%); may be permanent.
Confirm SNHL
Otoscopy normal; Weber → better ear; Rinne positive — not wax/effusion.
Imaging
MRI (IAM) in all cases to exclude ACOUSTIC NEUROMA (+ stroke/demyelination).
Management
Immediate ENT referral (<24 h) + HIGH-DOSE ORAL STEROIDS ASAP (best <2 weeks; useless after ~6 weeks) — don’t wait for the MRI.
Intratympanic
Salvage (or primary if systemic steroids contraindicated, e.g. diabetes).
Causes
Idiopathic, infection, Ménière’s, ototoxic drugs, multiple sclerosis, migraine, stroke, acoustic neuroma, Cogan’s syndrome.
Ototoxic mnemonic
“FAV Q&A” — Furosemide, Aminoglycosides, Vancomycin, Quinine/NSAIDs, Aspirin.
Prognosis
~50–65% recover; worse if older, severe loss, vertigo, delayed treatment.
What & Why

Otosclerosis is abnormal bone remodelling in the otic capsule of the middle ear — most importantly fixation of the stapes footplate at the oval window — causing progressive conductive hearing loss. It’s the commonest cause of progressive conductive hearing loss in young adults with a normal eardrum: the classic stem is a young adult (often a woman) with gradually worsening hearing, tinnitus, a family history, and a normal otoscopy — and it’s surgically curable (stapedectomy/stapedotomy).

Note on naming: the correct term is otosclerosis (“oto-” = ear), not “osteosclerosis” (which means dense bone generally).
The core mechanism: normal dense otic-capsule bone is resorbed and replaced by vascular, spongy (“spongiotic”) bone, then later dense sclerotic bone. Starting classically at the fissula ante fenestram (just anterior to the oval window), it spreads to fix the stapes footplate → the ossicular chain can’t vibrate → conductive hearing loss. (If it spreads into the cochlea → an added sensorineural component.)
The Decisive Fork — Stapedial vs Cochlear
Stapedial (commonest)Cochlear
SiteStapes footplate / oval windowSpread into the cochlea
LossConductiveSensorineural (mixed) component
RinneNegative (BC > AC) — conductiveDepends on SNHL degree
Epidemiology & Inheritance
  • Autosomal dominant with incomplete/variable penetrance — strong family history common
  • Young adults — onset typically 20–40 years
  • More common in women (~2:1) and Caucasians
  • Pregnancy (and hormonal changes) can trigger/accelerate it — may become apparent or worsen around pregnancy
  • Usually BILATERAL (~80%)
Clinical Features
  • Progressive (conductive) hearing loss — bilateral, gradual, painless
  • Tinnitus
  • Affects lower-pitched sounds more → “easier to hear female (higher-pitched) voices”
  • Paracusis Willisii — patients hear BETTER in noisy environments (people raise their voices, overcoming the conductive loss) — a hallmark of conductive loss
  • Soft, monotonous speech (they hear their own voice well by bone conduction, so speak quietly)
  • Vertigo is uncommon (helps distinguish from Ménière’s/inner-ear causes)
  • Normal tympanic membrane on otoscopy — the key exam point
Examination & Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Pure-tone audiogram of otosclerosis — a conductive air–bone gap with Carhart’s notch (bone-conduction dip at 2 kHz) that resolves after successful stapes surgery
  • Otoscopy: normal eardrum — occasionally a Schwartze sign (a reddish/pink hue over the promontory, seen through the drum) reflecting increased vascularity in the active otospongiotic phase
  • Tuning-fork tests: Rinne NEGATIVE (BC > AC) in the affected ear (conductive); Weber lateralises to the affected/worse ear
  • Pure-tone audiometry = gold standard: a conductive loss pattern (air–bone gap), with Carhart’s notch — a characteristic dip in the BONE-conduction curve at 2 kHz (an artefact of stapes fixation, not true cochlear loss; resolves after successful surgery)
  • Tympanometry: typically type A (or reduced compliance); absent stapedial (acoustic) reflexes (an early feature)
  • CT temporal bone — can show otospongiotic foci; used pre-op / if the diagnosis is unclear
Management
🦻 Conservative
  • Hearing aids — effective, non-surgical; a reasonable first-line for many
🔧 Surgery
  • Stapedotomy — a small hole in the stapes footplate + a prosthesis (footplate base largely left in place); now the preferred procedure (safer, fewer complications)
  • Stapedectomy — removal of the (whole) stapes, replaced with a prosthesis to the oval window
  • Cochlear implant — for advanced otosclerosis with severe sensorineural loss
  • Sodium fluoride — sometimes used to stabilise active otospongiotic disease (limited evidence)
  • Surgical risks: sensorineural loss/dead ear (small), dysgeusia (chorda tympani), vertigo, tinnitus — counsel the patient
Exam Pearls
What it is
Stapes footplate fixation at the oval window → progressive CONDUCTIVE loss; commonest cause in young adults with a NORMAL eardrum. (Not “osteosclerosis”.)
Epidemiology
Autosomal dominant (variable penetrance); onset 20–40; F>M; usually bilateral; worsens in PREGNANCY.
Features
Gradual painless conductive loss + tinnitus; affects low-pitched sounds (hears women’s voices better); vertigo uncommon.
Classic signs
Paracusis Willisii (hears better in noise); soft monotonous speech.
Otoscopy
NORMAL — occasionally Schwartze sign (pink promontory, active phase).
Tuning forks
Rinne NEGATIVE (BC>AC) = conductive; Weber → worse ear.
Audiometry
Gold standard: conductive loss + air–bone gap + CARHART’S NOTCH (BC dip at 2 kHz). Absent stapedial reflexes.
Management
Hearing aids (conservative) or STAPEDOTOMY (preferred) / stapedectomy + prosthesis; cochlear implant if severe SNHL.
What & Why

Presbycusis is age-related sensorineural hearing loss — the cumulative effect of ageing on hearing. It’s the commonest cause of hearing loss overall and, although irreversible, has large, under-appreciated consequences: social isolation, depression, and an independent association with cognitive decline/dementia. Exam essence: a gradual, bilateral, symmetrical high-frequency SNHL in an older adult, diagnosed on audiometry, managed supportively with hearing aids — and recognising that treating it matters for more than just hearing.

The core mechanism: ageing degrades key cochlear structures — loss of cochlear hair cells (especially outer hair cells at the base, which detect high frequencies → why high tones go first); loss of cochlear (spiral ganglion) neurones; atrophy of the stria vascularis (the “metabolic pump” maintaining the endocochlear potential).
The Decisive Fork — Symmetrical SNHL vs Red Flags

Presbycusis is bilateral, symmetrical, and gradual — exactly what distinguishes it from sinister causes.

Presbycusis (reassuring)Red flags (investigate)
LateralityBilateral, symmetricalUnilateral / asymmetrical → acoustic neuroma, SSNHL
OnsetGradual, insidious (years)Sudden → SSNHL (emergency)
Associated± tinnitusVertigo, facial weakness, otorrhoea, pain → other pathology
Asymmetry, sudden onset, or associated neurological signs are NOT presbycusis — they mandate audiometry ± MRI to exclude acoustic neuroma or SSNHL.
Risk Factors
📷 Image placeholder — Contrasting audiograms — the noise-induced 4 kHz notch (recovering at 8 kHz) vs the symmetrical down-sloping high-frequency loss of presbycusis
  • Age (the primary driver)
  • Male sex; family history / genetics
  • Cumulative loud-noise exposure (accelerates it — overlaps with noise-induced loss)
  • Cardiovascular risk: diabetes, hypertension (reduce cochlear/strial blood supply)
  • Ototoxic drugs, smoking
Clinical Features
  • Gradual, insidious, bilateral hearing loss
  • High-pitched (high-frequency) sounds lost first → difficulty hearing/understanding speech, especially consonants (s, f, t, k) and especially in background noise (“I can hear but can’t make out what’s said”)
  • Male voices easier than female — presbycusis affects the high frequencies (female/children’s voices are higher-pitched). Opposite of otosclerosis (low frequencies → hears female voices more easily) — a nice exam contrast
  • Tinnitus may be present; ± “recruitment” (abnormal loudness growth — sudden sounds seem uncomfortably loud)
Investigations
  • Otoscopy — normal (excludes wax/effusion/other conductive causes)
  • Weber’s/Rinne’s — sensorineural pattern (Rinne positive/AC>BC bilaterally; Weber central if symmetrical)
  • Pure-tone audiometry — establishes the diagnosis: a bilateral, symmetrical, down-sloping high-frequency SNHL (both AC and BC depressed together, no air–bone gap)
  • Speech audiometry — quantifies speech-in-noise difficulty
Management
Irreversible — no cure; management is supportive/rehabilitative.
  • Optimise the listening environment — reduce background noise, face the person, speak clearly (not shout)
  • Hearing aids — the mainstay; amplify sound (especially high frequencies)
  • Cochlear implants — for severe/profound loss not helped by hearing aids
  • Assistive devices (amplified phones, loop systems, subtitles), lip-reading/communication support
  • Modify risk factors — protect from further noise, manage cardiovascular risk
  • Address the wider impact: screen for/manage social isolation and depression; treating hearing loss (hearing aids) may reduce the risk of cognitive decline/dementia — hearing loss is a recognised modifiable dementia risk factor, so early aiding is encouraged
Exam Pearls
What it is
Age-related, bilateral, symmetrical, gradual SENSORINEURAL loss; commonest cause of hearing loss overall.
Pathophysiology
Loss of cochlear hair cells (basal/outer → high frequencies first) + loss of cochlear neurones + atrophy of the stria vascularis.
Key feature
HIGH-frequency loss first → trouble understanding speech (consonants) in background noise; male voices easier than female. (Opposite of otosclerosis, which affects low frequencies.)
Risk factors
Age, male, family history, noise exposure, diabetes/hypertension, smoking, ototoxic drugs.
Audiometry
Bilateral symmetrical SNHL, down-sloping, worse at high frequencies, no air–bone gap.
Red flags
UNILATERAL/asymmetrical or SUDDEN loss is NOT presbycusis → exclude acoustic neuroma / SSNHL (MRI).
Management
Irreversible → supportive: environment optimisation + HEARING AIDS (mainstay); cochlear implant if severe.
Wider impact
Hearing loss is a modifiable DEMENTIA risk factor + causes social isolation/depression — treat it (aid early).
What & Why

Ear wax (cerumen) is a normal, physiological, protective substance in the outer ear canal — it lubricates, traps debris, is antibacterial, and is self-clearing (jaw movement migrates it outward). It matters clinically only when impacted — blocking the canal → hearing loss and other symptoms — an extremely common, benign, treatable primary-care presentation. Exam essence: recognise it as a cause of conductive hearing loss, know the removal methods, and know the contraindications to irrigation (perforation).

The core point: cerumen is protective and self-clearing — so do NOT routinely remove asymptomatic wax, and do not tell patients to use cotton buds (which push wax deeper and cause impaction). Treat only symptomatic impaction or to allow examination of the eardrum.
Clinical Features
  • Pain (otalgia) / a feeling of fullness or blockage
  • Conductive hearing loss (the commonest reason for removal)
  • Tinnitus; vertigo / dizziness
  • Also: itch, cough (vagal stimulation of the canal), and inability to examine the tympanic membrane
Key framing: impacted wax is a classic cause of conductive hearing loss — on Weber’s it lateralises to the affected (blocked) ear, and Rinne’s is negative (BC > AC) on that side.
Risk Factors for Impaction
  • Cotton bud use (pushes wax in — the big one)
  • Hearing aids / ear plugs / in-ear devices (block natural migration)
  • Narrow or hairy/tortuous ear canals, exostoses
  • Older age (drier wax), dermatological conditions of the canal (eczema)
Assessment
  • Otoscopy — confirms wax occluding the canal; assess the tympanic membrane where possible (exclude perforation, infection, or a cholesteatoma — wax obscuring the attic/pars flaccida can hide one)
  • Assess for hearing loss (screen it’s conductive with tuning-fork tests)
  • Ask about eardrum perforation, grommets, or previous ear surgery — this determines whether irrigation is safe
Management
1. Nothing, if asymptomatic — wax is protective and self-clears; only treat if symptomatic or to visualise the drum.
  • 2. First-line: cerumenolytic (softening) ear drops — olive oil, almond oil, sodium bicarbonate 5%, or water-based drops for ~3–5 days; often sufficient alone
  • 3. Ear irrigation (“syringing” — warm-water electronic irrigator) — if drops alone don’t clear it; often drops first to soften, then irrigate
  • 4. Microsuction — the gold-standard removal (a suction device under direct microscope vision); preferred where irrigation is contraindicated; dry, direct-vision, no water → safest
  • 5. Manual removal — a Jobson Horne probe / ring curette / crocodile forceps under direct vision (specialist)
Contraindications to irrigation: perforated tympanic membrane (current or previous), grommets / previous middle-ear surgery, only-hearing ear, active otitis externa / infection / discharge, previous pain/complication with irrigation, and (relative) young children → use microsuction instead.
Advice: do NOT use cotton buds; regular olive oil drops help those prone to build-up (e.g. hearing-aid users). Complications of removal: canal trauma/laceration, otitis externa, TM perforation, vertigo (cold water → caloric stimulation), rarely infection.
Exam Pearls
Cerumen
Normal, protective, self-clearing — only treat IMPACTED, SYMPTOMATIC wax (or to see the drum).
Impaction
→ conductive hearing loss (Weber → affected ear; Rinne negative), plus pain, fullness, tinnitus, vertigo, cough.
Cotton buds
Cause impaction — advise against them.
Ladder
Softening drops (olive oil/sodium bicarbonate, 3–5 days) → irrigation → microsuction/manual removal.
Irrigation contraindications
Perforation, grommets, previous ear surgery, only-hearing ear, active otitis externa → use MICROSUCTION (gold standard, direct vision, no water).
Always
Assess the TM — exclude perforation and cholesteatoma (attic wax) before treating.
Complications
Canal trauma, otitis externa, perforation, vertigo.
What & Why

Tinnitus is the perception of sound in the ears or head with no external source — classically a ringing, but also buzzing, hissing, or humming. It’s very common, usually benign (a symptom, not a disease), and the examinable skill is triage: identifying the few with red-flag features (a serious cause like an acoustic neuroma or vascular lesion) among the majority who need reassurance and hearing support. Tinnitus is often the companion of hearing loss — treat the hearing loss and it often improves.

The core framing: tinnitus is a surrogate for what’s happening in the auditory pathway — most often it reflects hearing loss (the brain “turns up the gain” on a deprived system). Two questions: (1) is there a dangerous cause (red flags)? (2) is there a treatable contributor, especially hearing loss or wax?
The Decisive Fork — Any Red Flags?
📷 Image placeholder — Tinnitus red-flag triage — unilateral/asymmetric, pulsatile, sudden SNHL, vertigo or neuro/visual signs → specialist referral ± imaging; symmetrical non-pulsatile with no signs → reassure, do not image
Red flags → specialist assessment:
  • Unilateral tinnitus (asymmetry → ?acoustic neuroma)
  • Pulsatile tinnitus (→ vascular cause — needs imaging)
  • Associated unilateral / asymmetric hearing loss
  • Sudden-onset hearing loss (→ emergency — SSNHL)
  • Associated vertigo or dizziness; hyperacusis (distressing sound sensitivity)
  • Headaches or visual symptoms, or associated neurological symptoms
  • Suicidal ideation related to tinnitus (→ urgent psychological support)
Classification
  • Subjective (only the patient hears it — the vast majority) vs objective (a real sound the examiner can detect — rare, e.g. vascular bruit, palatal myoclonus)
  • Pulsatile (rhythmic, in time with the heartbeat → vascular — always investigate) vs non-pulsatile (continuous — usually benign/auditory)
Aetiology / Causes
  • Idiopathic (most common — often with age-related hearing loss)
  • Hearing loss — noise-induced and presbycusis
  • Impacted ear wax — easily seen on otoscopy (a reversible cause)
  • Ménière’s disease — fluctuating hearing loss + vertigo + tinnitus + aural fullness
  • Otosclerosis — onset 20–40, conductive deafness, tinnitus, normal tympanic membrane
  • Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) — unilateral hearing loss, vertigo, tinnitus, absent corneal reflex; associated with neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)
  • SSNHL — mostly idiopathic; an emergency
  • Drugs (ototoxic) — aspirin/NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, loop diuretics (bumetanide/furosemide), quinine (± cisplatin)
Investigations
  • Bloods: FBC (anaemia), glucose/HbA1c, TSH (thyroid), lipids — screen for contributory systemic causes
  • Audiological assessment (pure-tone audiometry) — for most patients (identify hearing loss)
  • Imaging: pulsatile → imaging (MRI/MR angiography or contrast CT head/neck) for a vascular cause; non-pulsatile with neuro/otological/head-and-neck signs, or unilateral/asymmetric → MRI of the internal auditory meati (IAM) (acoustic neuroma)
  • Do NOT image symmetrical, non-pulsatile tinnitus with no associated signs (benign — avoid unnecessary scans)
  • Validated impact tools (e.g. Tinnitus Functional Index) to gauge severity/distress
Management
  • Investigate and treat any underlying cause — remove wax, review ototoxic drugs, manage Ménière’s
  • Reassurance and education — common, usually benign, many habituate; stress and poor sleep amplify the perception
  • Amplification / hearing aids — offer if there’s a hearing loss affecting communication. Do NOT offer hearing aids to people with tinnitus but no hearing loss
  • Sound therapy — background/environmental sound to reduce the contrast of the tinnitus (e.g. low-level sound at night)
  • Psychological therapy — CBT — for significant tinnitus-related distress (best-evidenced for distress)
  • Tinnitus support groups and self-help (e.g. British Tinnitus Association); manage associated insomnia, anxiety, or depression
Exam Pearls
What it is
Perception of sound with no external source; usually benign, often reflects HEARING LOSS.
Red flags
Refer: UNILATERAL, PULSATILE, sudden/asymmetric hearing loss, vertigo, hyperacusis, neuro/visual symptoms, suicidal ideation.
Imaging
Pulsatile = vascular → always image. Unilateral/asymmetric non-pulsatile → MRI IAM (acoustic neuroma).
Don’t over-image
Don’t image symmetrical non-pulsatile tinnitus with no other signs.
Causes
Presbycusis/noise, wax, Ménière’s, otosclerosis, acoustic neuroma, SSNHL, ototoxic drugs (aspirin, aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, quinine).
Work-up
Bloods: FBC, glucose, TSH, lipids. Audiometry for most.
Management
Treat the cause + reassurance + hearing aids (only if hearing loss) + sound therapy + CBT (distress) + support groups.
Hearing aids
Only if there’s a hearing loss — not for tinnitus alone.
Acoustic neuroma clues
Unilateral tinnitus + hearing loss + absent corneal reflex + NF2.
ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disorders:
Overview — vertigo & balance disorders
The illusion of movement (vertigo) from vestibular pathology — peripheral (labyrinth/vestibular nerve) is far commoner than central. The big three are BPPV, vestibular neuritis and Ménière's.
The organising principle: duration + trigger + associated features. BPPV = seconds, positional (Dix-Hallpike); vestibular neuritis = days, constant, post-viral, no hearing loss; Ménière's = episodic (minutes–hours) vertigo + hearing loss + tinnitus + aural fullness.
ConditionDuration / triggerKey feature & treatment
BPPVseconds, positionalDix-Hallpike positive → Epley manoeuvre
Ménière's diseaseminutes–hours, episodicvertigo + fluctuating hearing loss + tinnitus + fullness; salt restriction, betahistine

Distinguish peripheral from central vertigo — central features (other neurology, gaze-evoked/direction-changing nystagmus, normal head-impulse test, new headache) → urgent imaging for posterior-circulation stroke. The HINTS exam helps.
What & Why

BPPV is the commonest cause of vertigo — brief episodes of spinning triggered by changes in head position (rolling over in bed, looking up, bending down). It’s very common, benign, and dramatically treatable with a bedside repositioning manoeuvre (the Epley), and is the classic peripheral vertigo that must be distinguished from dangerous central causes (posterior circulation stroke). Core: positional, seconds-long vertigo with NO hearing loss → Dix-Hallpike to diagnose → Epley to treat.

The core mechanism: tiny calcium carbonate crystals (otoconia / “otoliths”) normally sit in the utricle. They become dislodged and fall into a semicircular canal — most often the posterior canal (~85–95%). When the head moves, these free-floating particles (canalithiasis) drag the endolymph and deflect the cupula after gravity has settled them → a false signal of rotation → a brief burst of vertigo + nystagmus starting a moment after the movement, settling within a minute — explaining the latency, brief duration, fatiguability, and position-triggering.
The Decisive Fork — Peripheral or Central?

Before diagnosing BPPV, place the vertigo correctly — the crucial safety step is not missing a central (brainstem/cerebellar) cause.

FeaturePeripheral (e.g. BPPV)Central (stroke, tumour, MND/demyelination)

DurationShort (seconds–minutes)Persistent

CoordinationIntactImpaired (ataxia)
NauseaMore severeMilder
NystagmusUnilateral, horizontal (± torsional)Bilateral or vertical
Neuro signsNoneDiplopia, dysarthria, limb/CN signs
HINTS exam: Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew — used in acute persistent vertigo to separate peripheral from central. Counterintuitively, in peripheral vertigo the head impulse test is abnormal (a corrective saccade), whereas a normal head impulse with vertical/bidirectional nystagmus or skew deviation points to a central/stroke cause.
Clinical Features
  • Brief episodes of rotational vertigo (spinning), lasting <1 minute (typically 10–30 seconds)
  • Triggered by head-position change: rolling over in bed, lying down/sitting up, looking up (“top-shelf vertigo”), bending forward
  • Nausea ± vomiting, unsteadiness between attacks
  • NO hearing loss, NO tinnitus, NO aural fullness — a key discriminator (distinguishes from Ménière’s and labyrinthitis)
  • No continuous symptoms, no neurological signs — their presence → suspect a central cause (posterior circulation stroke)
  • Often follows head trauma, prolonged bed rest, or a viral labyrinthitis; commoner with age
Investigations — the Dix-Hallpike Manoeuvre
📷 Image placeholder — Dix-Hallpike positioning (head 45° to the test side, rapid supine with head hanging 20–30°) with the expected latent, fatiguable torsional-upbeating nystagmus
  • Dix-Hallpike test — the gold-standard diagnostic manoeuvre for posterior canal BPPV: patient sits upright, head turned 45° to the side being tested, then rapidly lie supine with the head extended ~20–30° below the couch (“head-hanging”), affected ear down
  • Positive result: after a short latency (a few seconds), a burst of rotational (torsional) upbeating nystagmus + vertigo that is transient (<1 min) and fatiguable on repetition
  • Supine roll test — if history suggests BPPV but Dix-Hallpike is negative → tests the horizontal (lateral) canal
  • MRI/imaging only if a central cause is suspected (atypical nystagmus, neuro signs, non-fatiguing) — not routine
Management
  • Epley manoeuvre — the treatment of choice (a canalith repositioning procedure): a sequence of head/body positions that rolls the otoconia out of the posterior canal and back into the utricle. >90% effective, often in one or two sessions
  • Brandt-Daroff exercises — home exercises for incomplete manoeuvres or recurrence; Semont manoeuvre — an alternative repositioning technique
  • Reassurance — BPPV is benign and often self-limiting (settles over weeks), but manoeuvres speed recovery; no post-Epley postural restrictions needed (old advice, now dropped)
  • Vestibular sedatives (e.g. prochlorperazine) are NOT recommended for BPPV — they don’t treat the mechanical cause and can worsen/prolong it; they’re for the acute nausea of other vertigo (neuritis/labyrinthitis), not BPPV
  • Refer if diagnosis uncertain, atypical, or not resolving with manoeuvres
Exam Pearls
What it is
Commonest vertigo; brief (<1 min) POSITIONAL spinning from displaced otoconia in the (usually posterior) semicircular canal (canalithiasis).
Trigger
Head movement (rolling in bed, looking up); nausea; NO hearing loss/tinnitus (key vs Ménière’s/labyrinthitis).
Diagnose
Dix-Hallpike → latent, transient, fatiguable torsional-upbeating nystagmus + vertigo.
Treat
EPLEY manoeuvre (canalith repositioning, >90% effective); Brandt-Daroff/Semont alternatives.
Sedatives
NOT for BPPV (only for acute neuritis/labyrinthitis nausea).
Peripheral vs central
Unilateral horizontal nystagmus + intact coordination + no neuro signs = peripheral; vertical/bidirectional nystagmus, ataxia, or CN signs = central (stroke) → image.
HINTS
Abnormal head impulse = reassuring (peripheral); normal head impulse + vertical nystagmus/skew = central.
Golden rule
No hearing loss and a normal neuro exam are what make it benign.
What & why
Ménière's disease = a chronic inner-ear disorder — the triad of episodic vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss, and tinnitus, with aural fullness — caused by endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph in the inner ear).
The core concept: the diagnosis is the classic triad + ear fullness, in episodic attacks lasting minutes–hours, on a background of fluctuating then progressive sensorineural hearing loss. It sits within the wider peripheral vertigo differential — so the key skill is placing it correctly among the causes of vertigo (BPPV, vestibular neuronitis, labyrinthitis, acoustic neuroma) and distinguishing peripheral from central vertigo (the must-not-miss being a posterior circulation stroke).
  • Typically middle-aged adults; usually unilateral (initially); a relapsing condition that can significantly affect quality of life.
The decisive fork — peripheral vs central vertigo

A reassuringly peripheral picture = abnormal head impulse + unidirectional horizontal nystagmus + no skew.
The rule: peripheral vertigo = sudden, short-lived, ± hearing loss/tinnitus, intact coordination; central = persistent + other neurology → exclude stroke (also tumour, multiple sclerosis, vestibular migraine).

Pathophysiology
  • Endolymphatic hydrops: excess endolymph accumulates in the membranous labyrinth (impaired reabsorption/drainage) → distension → episodic dysfunction of the cochlea (hearing loss + tinnitus) and vestibular apparatus (vertigo).
  • This explains the fluctuating early course and the combined cochlear + vestibular symptoms.

The attack pattern: clusters of attacks over weeks, with periods of remission; between attacks the patient may be well (early), but hearing progressively declines over years. Nystagmus during attacks; drop attacks (Tumarkin crises) — sudden falls without warning — occur in later disease.
Assessment / investigations
  • Diagnosis is clinical — the characteristic triad + episodic pattern; usually a specialist (ENT) diagnosis.
  • Audiometry: confirms a sensorineural pattern of hearing loss (typically low-frequency, fluctuating early) — the key test.
  • Exclude other causes: MRI to exclude acoustic neuroma (unilateral SNHL) and central causes; the vertigo differential (BPPV → Dix-Hallpike; central → HINTS).
  • Rinne/Weber confirm sensorineural loss.
Management
The overarching principle: acute symptom relief (vestibular sedatives) + long-term prophylaxis (betahistine + lifestyle) + specialist input; inform DVLA.
  • Acute attack: vestibular sedatives / antiemetics — prochlorperazine (fast relief of vertigo/nausea), antihistamines (cyclizine, cinnarizine) — short-term only; reassurance, safe environment.
  • Prophylaxis: betahistine (a histamine analogue) — first-line to reduce attack frequency; lifestyle — low-salt diet, reduce caffeine/alcohol, avoid triggers (a mainstay); diuretics (e.g. thiazide) sometimes used to reduce endolymph.
  • Refractory (specialist): intratympanic steroids or intratympanic gentamicin (ablates vestibular function — but ototoxic, hearing-loss risk); surgery (endolymphatic sac decompression, labyrinthectomy).
  • Supportive: hearing aids (for progressive SNHL), vestibular rehabilitation, tinnitus support.
DVLA: patients must inform the DVLA and stop driving during active disease (sudden, unpredictable vertigo attacks) until symptoms are controlled.
Exam pearls
What it is
Episodic vertigo + sensorineural hearing loss + tinnitus + aural fullness, from endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph).
Attack pattern
Attacks last minutes–hours, recurrent, usually unilateral; hearing loss fluctuates then becomes progressive/permanent.
Peripheral vs central (HINTS)
Peripheral = sudden, short, ± hearing loss, intact coordination; central = persistent + other neurology → exclude stroke.
vs other peripheral causes
BPPV (seconds, positional, no hearing loss, Dix-Hallpike/Epley), vestibular neuronitis (no hearing loss), labyrinthitis (+ hearing loss), acoustic neuroma (gradual unilateral SNHL).
Investigations
Audiometry (sensorineural, low-frequency fluctuating); MRI to exclude acoustic neuroma.
Management
Acute → prochlorperazine/antihistamines (vestibular sedatives); prophylaxis → betahistine + low-salt diet; refractory → intratympanic steroids/gentamicin, surgery; hearing aids.
Other
Inform the DVLA (sudden vertigo attacks); usually specialist (ENT) managed.
What & Why

Vestibular neuritis and labyrinthitis are the two “acute, prolonged, viral-associated” causes of peripheral vertigo — a single sustained attack of spinning (lasting days, not seconds like BPPV) usually following a viral URTI. The crucial skills: distinguish the two by HEARING, and don’t miss a central mimic (posterior circulation stroke). One-liner: prolonged vertigo after a cold, NO hearing loss = vestibular neuritis; WITH hearing loss/tinnitus = labyrinthitis.

The core anatomy — the difference is location: vestibular neuritis = inflammation of the vestibular nerve (balance division of CN VIII) only → vertigo without hearing loss. Labyrinthitis = inflammation of the whole labyrinth (vestibular apparatus AND the cochlea) → vertigo WITH hearing loss/tinnitus.
The Decisive Fork — Is Hearing Affected?

  • History of recent viral URTI
  • Vertigo — acute, severe, and constant (not purely positional like BPPV, though worsened by head movement)
  • Nausea and vomiting; balance problems / unsteadiness
  • Duration: days (peaks early, then gradually improves over days–weeks as central compensation occurs)
  • Nystagmus — horizontal, unidirectional, fast phase towards the unaffected ear

  • Neurological symptoms → consider a CENTRAL cause (posterior circulation stroke), not neuritis
Investigations
  • Clinical diagnosis — history + examination
  • Head impulse test is POSITIVE (abnormal) in vestibular neuritis/labyrinthitis (a peripheral sign — a corrective saccade); a normal head impulse with vertical/direction-changing nystagmus or skew suggests a central cause
  • HINTS exam (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) — to distinguish peripheral (neuritis) from central (stroke) in acute persistent vertigo
  • Otoscopy + hearing assessment — to detect the hearing loss of labyrinthitis (and exclude middle-ear disease)
  • MRI if central features (neuro signs, normal head impulse, vertical nystagmus) → exclude stroke/tumour/demyelination
Management
💊 Acute symptom relief
  • Manage dehydration (IV fluids) if significant vomiting
  • Buccal or IM prochlorperazine for severe cases; short course of oral prochlorperazine or antihistamines (cyclizine, cinnarizine, promethazine) for less severe
  • Use only in the acute phase — stop after a few days — prolonged use delays recovery by interfering with central vestibular compensation (and increases fall risk)
🔄 Recovery / chronic
  • Vestibular rehabilitation exercises — the preferred treatment for chronic/persistent symptoms (retrains central compensation)
  • Advise not to drive while vertiginous or on sedating medication
Labyrinthitis-specific: sudden sensorineural hearing loss accompanying labyrinthitis → high-dose corticosteroids + urgent ENT referral (treat as SSNHL). Bacterial labyrinthitis (from otitis media/meningitis) → antibiotics + treat the source; risk of permanent hearing loss.
Corticosteroids and antivirals are NOT routinely recommended for uncomplicated vestibular neuritis (no proven symptom benefit) — VRT is the mainstay for recovery. Referral if symptoms don’t improve after ~1 week or don’t resolve by ~6 weeks.

Acute, prolonged (days) peripheral vertigo after a viral URTI, with N&V + unsteadiness.

HEARING: vestibular neuritis = NO hearing loss (nerve only); labyrinthitis = hearing loss/tinnitus (whole labyrinth incl. cochlea).

Fluids + short-course prochlorperazine/antihistamine (ACUTE ONLY — stop in days, they delay compensation) → vestibular rehabilitation for chronic symptoms.

Steroids/antivirals not routine in uncomplicated neuritis. Advise not to drive.
ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & Nasal Polyps:
Overview — rhinitis, sinusitis & nasal polyps
Inflammatory conditions of the nose and paranasal sinuses — allergic/non-allergic rhinitis, acute and chronic rhinosinusitis, and nasal polyps.
The organising principle: allergic vs infective vs chronic inflammatory. Allergic rhinitis (sneezing, itch, clear rhinorrhoea, atopy) vs sinusitis (facial pain/pressure, purulent discharge, mostly viral) vs chronic rhinosinusitis ± polyps.

Part A — Allergic Rhinitis · Part B — Sinusitis (Rhinosinusitis). Two overlapping “runny/blocked nose” topics — allergic rhinitis is IgE-driven; sinusitis is sinus inflammation from ostial blockage.
A · Allergic Rhinitis — What & Why

Allergic rhinitis is IgE-mediated inflammation of the nasal mucosa triggered by allergen exposure — the nasal counterpart of allergic conjunctivitis, and the “R” of the atopic march. It’s extremely common (“hay fever”), impairs QoL/sleep/concentration, frequently coexists with asthma and conjunctivitis (“one airway” — treating the nose helps the chest), and has a clean, examinable stepwise ladder.

The core mechanism: allergen (pollen, dust mite, dander) → binds IgE on nasal mast cells → degranulation → histamine + mediators → sneezing, itch, rhinorrhoea, congestion. Early phase (histamine — sneeze/itch/watery discharge) + late phase (cellular infiltrate — congestion) — why antihistamines and intranasal steroids are the mainstays.
A · Classification & Features
  • Seasonal (pollen — “hay fever”; grass/tree/weed) vs perennial (house dust mite, dander, mould); or intermittent vs persistent (ARIA), and mild vs moderate–severe (by impact)
  • Sneezing, nasal itch, watery rhinorrhoea, congestion/blockage; itchy watery eyes (allergic conjunctivitis), itchy palate/throat
  • Postnasal drip, reduced smell, mouth breathing/snoring; associated atopy (asthma, eczema, family history)
  • On exam: pale, boggy, oedematous nasal mucosa, clear discharge; children — “allergic salute”/nasal crease, allergic shiners
A · Investigations & Management

Clinical diagnosis (history + exam). Skin-prick testing or specific IgE (RAST) if the trigger is unclear or immunotherapy is considered.

  • 1. Allergen avoidance — reduce dust mite/pet/pollen; nasal saline irrigation
  • 2. Antihistamines — non-sedating oral (cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) or intranasal (azelastine); good for mild/intermittent + sneeze/itch/rhinorrhoea (less for congestion)
  • 3. Intranasal corticosteroids (fluticasone, mometasone, beclometasone) — the most effective single agent, first-line for moderate–severe/persistent symptoms (treat congestion too)
  • 4. Combination — intranasal steroid + antihistamine (azelastine/fluticasone spray) if inadequate control
  • 5. Add-ons: leukotriene receptor antagonist (montelukast, esp. with asthma); short oral steroid for severe flares; 6. allergen immunotherapy for refractory allergen-specific disease
Avoid prolonged topical decongestants (oxymetazoline >5–7 days) → rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound congestion).
B · Sinusitis (Rhinosinusitis) — What & Why

Sinusitis (correctly rhinosinusitis — the nose is always involved) is inflammation of the paranasal sinuses. Acute sinusitis is common and usually viral (so antibiotic stewardship is central), chronic rhinosinusitis impairs QoL, and there are rare but dangerous orbital/intracranial complications. Core: the 10-day antibiotic rule and the red flags.

The core mechanism: sinuses produce mucus that drains into the nasal cavity via the ostia. Blockage of the ostia (mucosal swelling after a viral URTI, allergy, polyps, foreign body, trauma) → disrupted drainage → mucus stagnation → inflammation/infection.

  • Most acute cases need NO investigation (clinical); persistent despite management → nasal endoscopy + CT sinuses (CT is imaging of choice for CRS)
  • Red flags → ENT referral: unilateral symptoms, persistent despite 3 months of management, epistaxis — exclude a tumour (nasopharyngeal/sinonasal carcinoma)

  • Back-up (delayed) antibiotic — phenoxymethylpenicillin (5 days) if worsening/no improvement in ~7 days — esp. “double-sickening”; immediate co-amoxiclav if very unwell
🔁 Chronic rhinosinusitis
  • Allergen avoidance; intranasal corticosteroids (long-term)
  • Saline nasal irrigation; treat contributing factors (allergy, smoking cessation)

Allergic rhinitis
IgE/mast-cell nasal inflammation → sneeze, itch, rhinorrhoea, congestion + itchy watery eyes. Pale boggy mucosa.
AR ladder
Avoidance → antihistamine → INTRANASAL CORTICOSTEROID (most effective, moderate-severe) → combination → montelukast/immunotherapy.
AR caution
Avoid decongestants >5–7 days → rhinitis medicamentosa.
Rhinosinusitis
Sinus inflammation from ostial blockage; acute <12 wks (mostly viral), chronic ≥12 wks (± polyps).
Sinusitis features
Facial pain/pressure WORSE ON BENDING FORWARD + congestion + discharge + reduced smell.
Acute Rx
≤10 days → NO antibiotics (analgesia). >10 days → high-dose nasal steroid (mometasone 14 days) ± delayed phenoxymethylpenicillin (“double-sickening”).
Red flags
Unilateral symptoms, epistaxis, symptoms >3 months → ENT (exclude tumour).
Complications
Orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, intracranial abscess, meningitis, Pott’s puffy tumour.
What & Why

Chronic rhinosinusitis is persistent inflammation of the nasal + paranasal sinus mucosa lasting ≥12 weeks. It’s common (~10% of the population), significantly impairs QoL (sleep, smell, productivity), and its management has been transformed by biologics for the severe polyp-forming type. It’s now organised by phenotype — with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) vs without (CRSsNP) — because this drives treatment.

The core mechanism: persistent mucosal inflammation + impaired mucociliary clearance + ostial obstruction → a self-perpetuating cycle of stasis, inflammation, and (often) infection. Driven by dysregulated immune responses (frequently type 2 / eosinophilic, especially with polyps) rather than a single infection.
Definition (EPOS Criteria)
CRS = ≥12 weeks of ≥2 symptoms, one of which must be nasal blockage/obstruction/congestion OR nasal discharge (anterior/posterior drip), ± facial pain/pressure, and/or reduction/loss of smell.

PLUS objective evidence — either endoscopic signs (polyps, mucopurulent discharge, or oedema/obstruction in the middle meatus) or CT changes (mucosal disease in the ostiomeatal complex/sinuses).

Predisposing Factors & Features
👤 Predisposing factors
  • Atopy/allergy; nasal obstruction (deviated septum, polyps)
  • Recent/recurrent local infection; swimming; smoking
  • Also: asthma, aspirin sensitivity, cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, immunodeficiency (esp. young/bilateral polyps)
🩺 Clinical features
  • Facial pain/pressure — worse on bending forward
  • Nasal discharge (anterior or postnasal drip); obstruction/congestion → mouth breathing
  • Postnasal drip → chronic cough; reduced/lost smell (esp. polyps)
  • Systemic upset/fever uncommon (suggests acute exacerbation/complication)
Investigations
  • Nasal endoscopy — polyps, discharge, middle-meatus oedema/obstruction
  • CT sinuses (paranasal) — imaging of choice: extent of mucosal disease, ostiomeatal complex, essential for surgical planning
  • Red flags → ENT: unilateral symptoms (exclude sinonasal/nasopharyngeal carcinoma), persistent despite 3 months, epistaxis; orbital/visual/neurological signs → urgent
  • Consider allergy testing; young + bilateral polyps → cystic fibrosis / ciliary function testing
Management
  • Conservative: allergen avoidance + manage contributing factors (smoking cessation, treat allergy/asthma); intranasal corticosteroids (mainstay — sprays, or drops/rinses for polyps); high-volume saline irrigation
  • Escalation: short course of oral corticosteroids (significant polyps/severe symptoms); treat bacterial exacerbation; long-term low-dose macrolides sometimes used in CRSsNP
  • Surgical: functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) — for disease refractory to maximal medical therapy (opens ostia, removes polyps, restores drainage); polyps recur in a substantial proportion
  • Biologics — dupilumab (anti-IL-4/13), omalizumab (anti-IgE), mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) — for severe uncontrolled CRSwNP despite medical therapy ± surgery; dupilumab has transformed severe CRSwNP care

What & Why

Nasal polyps are benign, oedematous swellings of the nasal/sinus mucosa that grow into the nasal cavity. They define CRS with nasal polyps (CRSwNP), cause troublesome nasal obstruction and anosmia, and link to important systemic associations (asthma, aspirin sensitivity, cystic fibrosis). The single most important rule: bilateral polyps are benign and GP-managed; a UNILATERAL polyp is a red flag for malignancy.

The core mechanism: polyps arise from chronic inflammation of the sinonasal mucosa — usually type 2 (Th2/eosinophilic) inflammation → mucosal oedema that prolapses into the nasal cavity as pale, grape-like swellings that grow slowly + gradually obstruct.
Associations
  • Chronic rhinosinusitis (polyps define CRSwNP); asthma
  • Cystic fibrosis — consider CF in a child/young patient with nasal polyps (polyps are rare in children → their presence is a red flag)
  • Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss)
  • Samter’s triad (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, AERD) = nasal polyps + asthma + aspirin/NSAID sensitivity
  • Allergic rhinitis, chronic infection
Clinical Features
  • Usually bilateral; symptoms of chronic rhinosinusitis
  • Nasal obstruction (difficulty breathing through the nose); snoring
  • Nasal discharge / rhinorrhoea / postnasal drip
  • Loss of sense of smell (anosmia/hyposmia) — a cardinal feature
  • On exam: pale/grey, mobile, insensate swellings (touching a polyp doesn’t hurt — unlike the very sensate turbinate)
Investigations
  • Anterior rhinoscopy with a nasal speculum — view polyps
  • Nasal endoscopy (specialist) — better visualisation + assessment
  • CT sinuses — extent/surgical planning (and if unilateral/atypical, to assess a mass)
  • Consider CF testing in young patients; allergy/asthma assessment

ENT__Head & Neck Cancer:
Overview — head & neck cancer
Malignancies of the upper aerodigestive tract — larynx, oral cavity/tongue, nasopharynx and beyond — mostly squamous cell carcinoma, linked to smoking, alcohol and HPV/EBV.
The organising principle: recognise the red flags for 2-week-wait referral — persistent hoarseness (>3 weeks), a neck lump, a non-healing oral ulcer, dysphagia, or unilateral otalgia/nasal symptoms.
CancerClueRisk factor

Oral cavity & tongue lesionsnon-healing ulcer / red-white patchsmoking, alcohol, betel → biopsy

What & Why

Laryngeal cancer is a malignancy of the larynx (voice box) — the commonest head & neck cancer, and >90% are squamous cell carcinomas (SCC) arising from the mucosal lining. It matters because it presents with a very common symptom — hoarseness — that is usually benign, so the examinable skill is knowing which hoarse voice is a red flag (and triggering an urgent cancer referral) versus the many benign causes. It’s strongly smoking- and alcohol-driven (largely preventable) and, when caught early (as glottic tumours often are, because they cause hoarseness early), it’s very treatable with voice preservation.

The core anatomy (why site matters): the larynx has three regions, and the site determines how early it presents and how it spreads.
🎯 Glottis (vocal cords) — commonest
  • Hoarseness appears EARLY (any cord lesion changes the voice) → often caught early
  • Poor lymphatic supply → spreads late (better prognosis)
Supraglottis / Subglottis
  • Supraglottis (above cords): presents later — sore throat, dysphagia, referred otalgia, neck lump; rich lymphatics → early nodal spread
  • Subglottis (below cords): rare, presents late with stridor/airway obstruction
The Decisive Fork — Is This Hoarse Voice a Red Flag?

Hoarseness (dysphonia) is the key symptom — most causes are benign, but you must screen for the sinister.

CategoryCauses
Benign / inflammatoryAcute laryngitis (viral/URTI — commonest), voice overuse/misuse (vocal cord nodules — “singer’s nodules”), vocal cord polyps

The rule: persistent hoarseness (>3 weeks), especially in a smoker/drinker over 45–50, is laryngeal cancer until proven otherwise → urgent referral.
Referral — NICE (2-Week-Wait)
Consider a suspected-cancer (2-week-wait) referral for laryngeal cancer in people aged 45 and over with: persistent unexplained hoarseness, OR an unexplained lump in the neck.

Also refer / urgently investigate: stridor → same-day; persistent sore throat/dysphagia, otalgia with a normal ear, haemoptysis, or an unexplained neck lump (cross-reference the NICE head & neck criteria).

Risk Factors
  • Smoking — the dominant factor (~90–95% of patients smoke; strong dose-response)
  • Alcohol (excess — synergistic with smoking)
  • Male sex, older age (60–70)
  • HPV (especially supraglottic; more established in oropharyngeal cancer)
  • Occupational exposures (asbestos, wood dust), lower socioeconomic status, previous radiotherapy, GORD/LPR
Clinical Features
  • Persistent hoarseness / voice change (dysphonia) — the cardinal symptom (early in glottic cancer)
  • Persistent sore throat, dysphagia or odynophagia
  • Referred otalgia (ear pain with a normal ear) — via the vagus nerve
  • Unexplained neck lump (nodal metastasis — especially supraglottic)
  • Stridor / dyspnoea (airway narrowing — an emergency sign)
  • Haemoptysis, weight loss, chronic cough; a globus sensation (overlaps with LPR)
Investigations
  • Flexible nasendoscopy / laryngoscopy — the key first-line examination (visualises the larynx/vocal cords, assesses cord mobility + any lesion)
  • Biopsy under direct (micro)laryngoscopy — for histological diagnosis (usually general anaesthetic)
  • Imaging for staging: CT/MRI neck + thorax (local extent + nodes + chest); PET-CT in some
  • Assess airway and swallowing; MDT staging (TNM)
Management

Managed by the head & neck MDT.

  • Early-stage (T1/T2), especially glottic: radiotherapy or transoral laser microsurgery — aiming for voice/organ preservation (excellent local control, ~90%+ for early glottic)
  • Advanced disease: chemoradiotherapy (organ-preservation) or surgery — partial or total laryngectomy (total laryngectomy leaves a permanent tracheostomy/stoma + need for voice rehabilitation)
  • Neck dissection for nodal disease
  • Smoking & alcohol cessation — essential (continuing worsens outcomes + second-tumour risk)
  • Voice/swallow rehabilitation (SALT), MDT support
Two Key “Hoarse Voice” Conditions
🔥 Laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR)
  • GORD-type acid reflux reaching the larynx → inflammatory change to the laryngeal mucosa
  • Features: globus (lump-in-throat) — worse swallowing SALIVA, not food/drink; hoarseness, chronic cough, dysphagia, heartburn; posterior pharynx may look erythematous; exam otherwise normal (no mass)
  • Management: lifestyle measures, PPI, sodium alginate (Gaviscon)
  • LPR is a diagnosis of exclusion — persistent hoarseness still needs the larynx visualised to rule out cancer
🧠 Recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) palsy
  • The RLN (a branch of the vagus) supplies the intrinsic laryngeal muscles → damage → vocal cord palsy → hoarse/breathy voice
  • The left RLN loops under the aortic arch (longer course) → more often affected; causes: lung cancer (apex), thyroid cancer/surgery, aortic aneurysm, mediastinal disease
  • An unexplained vocal cord palsy warrants imaging of the whole nerve course (skull base → mediastinum) to find the cause
Exam Pearls
What it is
Commonest head & neck cancer; >90% SCC; strongly smoking + alcohol driven.
Site
Glottic (commonest): hoarseness EARLY, spreads late (good prognosis). Supraglottic: presents late (sore throat/dysphagia/otalgia/neck lump), early nodal spread. Subglottic: stridor.
2WW referral
NICE: ≥45 with persistent unexplained hoarseness OR unexplained neck lump. (Stridor → same-day.)
Golden rule
Persistent hoarseness >3 weeks in a smoker/drinker = laryngeal cancer until proven otherwise.
Red flags
Referred otalgia (normal ear), neck lump, dysphagia, stridor, haemoptysis, weight loss.
Investigate
Nasendoscopy → microlaryngoscopy + biopsy → CT/MRI staging.
Treatment
Early glottic → radiotherapy / transoral laser (voice preservation); advanced → chemoradiotherapy or laryngectomy (+ stoma).
Hoarse differentials
Laryngitis, vocal nodules/polyps, LPR, RLN palsy, hypothyroidism, inhaled steroids, cancer.
LPR
Globus worse swallowing SALIVA, normal exam → PPI/Gaviscon — but exclude cancer first.
Left RLN palsy
Think lung/thyroid/mediastinal disease (loops under the aortic arch).
What & Why

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a squamous cell carcinoma arising from the epithelium of the nasopharynx (the space behind the nose, above the soft palate). It stands apart from other head & neck cancers because it has a completely distinctive profile: strongly linked to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a striking geographic/ethnic distribution (endemic in Southern China / SE Asia), a younger age group, and it is highly radiosensitive (so radiotherapy, not surgery, is the mainstay). The examinable trap: it presents with vague, “innocent” ENT symptoms (a blocked ear, a nosebleed, a neck lump) that get dismissed → often diagnosed late.

The core anatomy: NPC classically arises in the fossa of Rosenmüller (a recess in the lateral nasopharyngeal wall). Its position explains the whole presentation: near the Eustachian tube (→ blocks it → unilateral middle-ear effusion), near the nasal cavity (→ obstruction/epistaxis), rich in lymphatics (→ early neck-node spread — often the first sign), and near the skull base/cranial nerves (→ cranial nerve palsies).

  • Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) — the major aetiological agent (raised EBV serology / EBV DNA)

  • Diet — salt-preserved foods/salted fish (nitrosamines), especially in childhood
  • Genetic predisposition (HLA associations, family history)
  • Smoking, occupational exposures (formaldehyde, wood dust)
Clinical Features

The “innocent-looking” symptoms — often unilateral.

  • Neck lump (cervical lymphadenopathy) — the commonest presenting feature (often the first sign; upper/posterior cervical nodes)
  • Unilateral serous otitis media / middle-ear effusion — from Eustachian tube obstruction; a persistent unilateral middle-ear effusion in an adult is NPC until proven otherwise
  • Nasal symptoms — unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis, or blood-stained nasal discharge
  • Cranial nerve palsies — from skull-base invasion (e.g. diplopia (CN VI), facial numbness (CN V)) → often indicates advanced disease
  • Headache, otalgia, conductive hearing loss (from the effusion)
  • Trotter’s triad (classic): conductive deafness + ipsilateral facial/temporal pain (CN V3) + palatal palsy

  • Nasendoscopy — visualise the nasopharynx / fossa of Rosenmüller
  • Biopsy — histological diagnosis (nasopharyngeal biopsy)
  • EBV markers — EBV serology / plasma EBV DNA (diagnosis, monitoring, and in some regions screening)
  • Imaging: MRI (nasopharynx/skull base — best for local extent) + CT; PET-CT for staging/distant disease
  • Assess the neck — an unexplained neck lump may prompt a 2WW head & neck referral, but avoid excisional lymph node biopsy of a neck node before the primary is found (find the primary first — FNA/core if needed)
Management

Managed by the head & neck MDT.

  • Radiotherapy is the mainstay — NPC is highly radiosensitive, and its location makes surgery difficult; intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) to the primary + neck
  • Concurrent chemoradiotherapy (+ platinum-based chemo) for locally advanced disease
  • Surgery has a limited role (mainly salvage for residual/recurrent nodal or local disease — e.g. neck dissection)
  • Distant metastasis (bone, lung, liver) → systemic chemotherapy ± immunotherapy
  • Prognosis depends heavily on stage; early disease has good outcomes, but late presentation is common; EBV DNA levels help monitor response/recurrence

Neck lump (nodal spread).
High-yield red flag
Persistent UNILATERAL middle-ear effusion (serous otitis media) in an adult = NPC until proven otherwise (Eustachian tube obstruction).
Also
Unilateral nasal obstruction/epistaxis, cranial nerve palsies (skull-base invasion), Trotter’s triad.
Investigate
Nasendoscopy + biopsy; EBV DNA/serology; MRI nasopharynx/skull base; PET-CT staging.
Treatment
RADIOTHERAPY (± chemotherapy) — radiosensitive; surgery has a limited role.
Golden rule
Don’t excise a neck node before finding the primary — investigate for an occult primary (NPC) first.
What & Why

Oral cavity lesions span a huge range — from trivial and self-limiting (aphthous ulcers, geographic tongue) to premalignant (leukoplakia, erythroplakia) to frank cancer (oral squamous cell carcinoma). The mouth is easily examinable yet oral cancer is frequently caught late. The organising question is always: is this benign, premalignant, or malignant — and does it meet 2-week-wait criteria?

The core thread: most oral cancers are squamous cell carcinomas (SCC), driven by smoking, alcohol, and betel/areca nut, and many are preceded by a visible premalignant patch (leukoplakia/erythroplakia) — so recognising and biopsying the premalignant lesion is a chance to intervene early.
The Decisive Fork — Benign vs Premalignant vs Malignant
📷 Image placeholder — Leukoplakia (fixed white patch, won’t wipe off) vs erythroplakia (red velvety patch, much higher malignant potential) — both mandate biopsy
CategoryExamplesAction
Benign / self-limitingAphthous ulcers, geographic tongue, candidiasis, gingivitis, traumatic ulcerReassure / treat cause
PremalignantLeukoplakia, erythroplakia, oral lichen planus, submucous fibrosisBiopsy — assess dysplasia
